chapter: Wax Records, Broadway shows and Eddie Condon
title: The failed Philadelphia distribution deal for Wax Records
summary: Shellac shortages and a distributor who cancelled a thousand records when he saw Nicky.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Then what happened to Wax Records? According to the (inaudible), the calendar was taken over by Atlantic?
That was later, we couldn't get, it was during the war years, shellac was sparse, the sides were scratchy and the subject matter wasn't acceptable at that time, the jazz --
(Inaudible) was post-war, really.
Well, yeah, but still, it was still --
Still a problem to get --
Jazz --
Oh, no, I mean, I was talking about the mechanical part of it.
Oh, well, it was, yeah, it was post-war
but it was still --
The materials were still --
Yeah, yeah, still the 78's.
Yeah.
Wire tape had just come into vogue, regular tape just before.
All during that whole '45 to '50 period
it was wire.

Yeah, but that was mostly voice rather than music. And then, we thought we had a breakthrough on wax. I went to Philadelphia, the home boy sort of thing. I went to the Phoenix one record store, so he said, well, instead of selling me a record why don't you let me be (inaudible) the distributor and then I can get them on consignment, so I went to the distributor and played my records for him, he liked it, I think they ordered a thousand records which were to be delivered so we are doing this door to door sort of style, you know.
Yeah.

So, this particular day, we bring the thousand records to Philly and Nicky, she had her father's car, and we brought the records so I told her to go eat lunch while I (inaudible) took them on in, and I unloaded all the records and she got impatient and she came over and when they saw her --
Yeah, that was it.
They cancelled all of them. So then, we had to get a lawyer to get the shipment back.
What do you mean? They didn't give you the records back?

No. And, not only that, they took off records off the top of the cartons because this same fellow that had the record store had a copy of it and my father heard it and I had him to buy it and get a receipt for it.
To prove that --
